verses.text: Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives
when they see your pure and reverent demeanor.
Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes,
but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God's sight.
For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands,
just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.
Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.
Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.
Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.
For, "Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech.
He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it.
For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good?
But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. "Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken."
But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,
keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.
For it is better, if it is God's will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.
For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit,
in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison
who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.
And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,
who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.

context.author: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ (1:1). He writes with Silvanus, who may have been his secretary, the carrier of the letter, or both (5:12).
context.genre: Letter of encouragement to suffering believers
context.audience: Believers scattered across five Roman provinces in what is now Turkey (1:1). Verses such as 1:14, 1:18 and 4:3 suggest many were Gentiles by background, though Peter uses names once given to Israel.
context.setting: Peter addresses wives, including those with unbelieving husbands, and husbands. Then he turns to all believers: be of one mind, do not repay evil for evil, and always be ready to give a defense for the hope that is in you. It is better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil, as Christ did.
context.custom: In the Roman world a household was expected to follow the gods of its head, so a wife who turned to Christ while her husband did not was in a hard position. Peter advises quiet, respectful conduct that can win him without words. Noah and the flood in vv.20-21 become a picture of baptism, a passage through water to a clear conscience toward God.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 4 continues with arming oneself for suffering.
context.timelineBible: Sarah calling Abraham “lord” (v.6) refers to Genesis 18:12. Verses 10-12 quote Psalm 34:12-16. Verse 14-15 echoes Isaiah 8:12-13. Verses 19-20 refer to Noah (Genesis 6-8).
context.sparkNotes: Wives, be submissive to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won by your conduct. Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way. Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love. Do not repay evil for evil. Even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. In your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.

translation.meaning: A reasoned answer, as in a courtroom.

otBackground.note: Whoever wants life must keep the tongue from evil and do good. Quoted in 3:10-12.
Noah and the flood. Peter mentions the eight people saved through water (3:20).
Do not fear what they fear, but honor the Lord as holy. Compare 3:14-15.

overview.summary: Believers live well in households, bless those who wrong them, and are ready to explain their hope. Christ suffered for sins to bring us to God.
overview.settingLine: Peter writes from “Babylon” to believers in Asia Minor.

history.t: Genesis 6-8 says that Noah's family of eight went into the ark and came through the flood. Peter says that only eight souls were saved through water (3:20). Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, the region the Assyrians called Urartu.

Peter says that Christ went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in the days of Noah (3:19-20). Readers hold three main views: that Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day (Augustine took this view); that Christ proclaimed his victory to fallen angels, linked to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Jewish book of 1 Enoch; or that Christ preached to the dead between his death and resurrection. Peter does not explain, and the passage is one of the hardest in the New Testament.

In the Roman world a household was expected to follow the gods of its head. Plutarch, in his advice to a bride and groom (chapter 19), says a wife ought to worship the gods her husband recognizes. A wife who turned to Christ while her husband did not was in a hard position, and Peter speaks to her case (3:1-2).

customs.t: Women of rank in the Flavian period (AD 69-96) wore tall curled and braided hairstyles built up with added hair, and gold jewelry and fine clothes showed wealth. Peter says a woman's beauty should not come from them but from within (3:3-4).
The Greek word in 3:15 is apologia, the word for a defense given in answer to a charge or a question (Acts 22:1; 25:16). Peter ties it to a gentle and respectful tone.

Jewish ritual washings were common, and John's baptism preceded Jesus' (Mark 1:4-5). Peter says baptism saves by the pledge of a clear conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, not by removing dirt from the body (3:21).

archaeology.t: Portrait busts of women from the Flavian period show tall curled hairstyles. The bust in Munich is dated to about AD 80, a little after Peter wrote.

Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BC), tells of a man who builds a boat and saves his family and living creatures from a flood. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9 and debate how the stories are related. Peter does not refer to it.
The house church at Dura-Europos in Syria, from the 3rd century, has the oldest known Christian baptistery. It is about two centuries after Peter, but it shows how the early church practiced baptism.

overview.discussion: Peter says to always be ready to explain our hope “with gentleness and respect.” How would I answer if someone asked me today why I have hope?
overview.book: The first letter of Peter · 5 chapters. Encouragement to live as “exiles” with a living hope.

historicalImage.caption: A marble bust of a Roman woman, about AD 80, in the Glyptothek in Munich. Tall hairstyles built up with curls and added hair were fashionable at court and beyond in the Flavian period, a little after Peter wrote. Peter tells wives that their beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes (3:3).

currentImage.caption: Mount Ararat, with Great and Little Ararat, seen across the Ararat plain in Armenia. Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, the region the Assyrians called Urartu. The volcano now called Ararat is one traditional candidate, but the Bible names a range of mountains and not this peak.
